cells.tense: You're walking on partial light right now, and it's enough for the next step.
cells.ask: Pick the next thing you're stepping into and decide how much time it gets this week, then hold that without letting the schedule turn into a whip.
cells.core:
There's a stretch of your life where you move before you can see the whole way, and you're good at it. You feel what's coming and act on the feel instead of waiting for the fog to lift, and it's working. What could carry further now is staying warm on purpose. Choose the next thing you're stepping into, give it a real number of hours this week, and keep that steady.

Holding steady is hard because a fire tended too tightly goes out. You can feel the moment care turns into watching. The ask isn't to stop caring about what you're walking toward. It's to let the direction come from what you actually feel rather than from a rule about how you're supposed to feel, and to keep showing up for it without checking on it every hour.
cells.sheetLine: You move through fog well, and the next work is keeping a fire without burning it.
cells.verb: opening to what can't be felt yet — letting what's in the fog be felt before it's understood
cells.place: the part of a life where you move without being able to see the whole way at once

cells.tense: You're already braced for a version of this that hasn't arrived, and the fog keeps shifting before you can land on it.
cells.ask: Name the smallest real piece of this thing in front of you, one plain step you can take this week, and do that one rather than planning the whole route.
cells.core:
In the part of your life you navigate without a map, this goes well when you feel your way forward and the path shows up as you go, a few steps visible and the rest waiting. The fog isn't being trusted, it's being patrolled. If you can't see the whole route, you plan it anyway, ahead of any feeling, running every branch in your head until you're exhausted, and the running starts to feel like progress.

The tiredness has a shape. You're trying to hold the whole road in your mind at once, which is what makes it unholdable. What you want may really be there and you're trying to force it to show on schedule. Let one piece of it be developed slowly, the way you'd tend a plant on a windowsill, water and light and time, no pulling at the stem. Pick the smallest real piece of this and give it a week of ordinary care instead of a plan.
cells.sheetLine: You're hauling the whole route into view when the fog only shows the next few steps.
cells.verb: opening to what can't be felt yet — letting what's in the fog be felt before it's understood
cells.place: the part of a life where you move without being able to see the whole way at once

cells.tense: You're holding at the edge, looking back at a door that already closed, and the fog ahead hasn't been entered yet.
cells.ask: Look at one foggy thing — a job direction, a conversation, a move — and write three sentences about what it might feel like if it went well, before you judge any of it.
cells.core:
In some stretch of your life you move on partial light and it works. You've had times when the next step showed up as you took it. Lately you still notice, quietly, but the entering has gone. You can feel the fog and you're not walking into it. You wait for it to lift before you move, and you don't say so out loud.

Nothing is wrong with how you see. What's missing is one honest perception put down in front of you, a thing you notice and set out where you can look at it. So take one foggy thing and write three plain sentences about what it might feel like if it went well. Not the plan, the feel. Your perceptions land without argument once they're out. They just need something to land on.
cells.sheetLine: You can feel the fog, and you're not letting yourself walk into it.
cells.verb: opening to what can't be felt yet — letting what's in the fog be felt before it's understood
cells.place: the part of a life where you move without being able to see the whole way at once

cells.tense: You're already opening to what can't be felt yet — the fog-shape of it moves through your reading of people and events — while calling it something else.
cells.ask: Sit with one page of notes for ten minutes, no plan and no output, then say out loud, in words you choose, one thing you noticed about where this is heading.
cells.core:
There's a stretch of your life where you navigate fog. You feel your way toward what's coming and act on it, and you do it well. The trouble is you credit it to analysis or discipline or just being careful, the way a person calls a hunch 'that restaurant looked busy.' Your reading of what hasn't happened yet is doing daily work and getting filed under a name that hides it.

A page of notes is enough to make it visible. Ten minutes, no output, no plan, and then one sentence out loud about what you noticed. That small piece of sitting-with-it brings you back to what's already happening rather than sending you looking for proof. The reading was already accurate. It just wasn't signed.
cells.sheetLine: You call it analysis, and it's already the fog-shape you're reading.
cells.verb: opening to what can't be felt yet — letting what's in the fog be felt before it's understood
cells.place: the part of a life where you move without being able to see the whole way at once

attempts.check: The draft's riskiest personal claim is that the person has stopped opening to things they can't feel yet — the card only says the capacity is under-expressed, not what happened or why it went quiet, so every line stays at the level of what this capacity does, never at the level of this person's history. A reader could reasonably push back with 'I open to plenty, just not this' — which is fine, because the ask only asks for one look written down, not for a verdict about them. The ask survives being wrong: writing what the fog might be hiding teaches something about what they can imagine even if my read of the restraint is off. The sentence that serves the writer more than the reader is anything invoking 'the trust' or 'the wonder' as a thing they should feel — cut on sight.
